etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English *adoren, aouren, from Old French adorer, aorer, from Latin adōrō (“I pray to”), from ad (“to”) + ōrō (“I speak”).

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: Now, gods that we adore, whereof comes this?

quote.citation: 1758, Tobias Smollett, A Complete History of England, London: James Rivington and James Fletcher, 3rd edition, Volume 6, Book 8, “William III,” p. 29,[1]
quote.text: [James] was met at the castle-gate by a procession of  […]  bishops and priests in their pontificals, bearing the host, which he publicly adored.

quote.citation: 1852, Frederick Oakeley (translator), “O Come, All Ye Faithful” in Francis H. Murray, A Hymnal for Use in the English Church,[2]
quote.text:
Come and behold him
Born the King of Angels:
O come, let us adore Him,
Christ the Lord.

definitions.definition: To love with one's entire heart and soul; regard with deep respect and affection.

quote.citation: 1849, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter V, in The History of England from the Accession of James II, volume I, London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC, page 388:
quote.text: The great mass of the population abhorred Popery and adored Monmouth.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter II, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: "I ought to arise and go forth with timbrels and with dances; but, do you know, I am not inclined to revels? There has been a little—just a very little bit too much festivity so far …. Not that I don't adore dinners and gossip and dances; not that I do not love to pervade bright and glittering places. […]"

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto XI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  and likewise on her hedA Chapelet of sundry flowers she wore,From vnder which the deawy humour shed,Did tricle downe her haire, like to the horeCongealed litle drops, which doe the morne adore.
